records.sourceFile: How mental health affects injury risk and outcomes in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Rogers DL, Tanaka MJ, Cosgarea AJ, Ginsburg RD, Dreher GM. How Mental Health Affects Injury Risk and Outcomes in Athletes. Sports Health. 2023.
paper.abstract: This clinical review summarises how mental health disorders and symptoms occur in athletes, and how they relate to injury risk and recovery. It also reviews evidence that injury can worsen mental health and describes barriers to care such as stigma and limited clinical resources. The authors conclude that physical and mental health are closely linked in athletes and that screening and support systems need to improve.
paper.tldr: Athletes with anxiety, depression or high life stress appear to have higher injury risk and slower recovery, and injuries can in turn worsen mental health. Screening and access to clinicians with sport experience are the practical priorities the review identifies.
paper.methods: Clinical review. The authors state they searched PubMed for pertinent peer-reviewed studies. No inclusion criteria, screening process or quality appraisal are described.
paper.findings: In a cohort of 307 athletes at the 2015 IAAF World Championships, reporting a physical illness symptom that caused anxiety was associated with about five times the odds of injury during the event (odds ratio 5.6, 95% CI 1.3-23). In a preseason cohort of collegiate athletes, preseason anxiety was associated with higher subsequent injury rates (rate ratio 2.3, 95% CI 2.0-2.6). The review also reports that depression and stress were associated with poorer performance and with delayed or reduced return to sport in cited studies.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative clinical review with a single-database search and no described selection or quality criteria. The injury-link studies it cites are mostly observational cohorts and surveys, and the authors note that the true prevalence of mental health disorders is hard to measure. Causal direction between mental health and injury cannot be established from these data.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports medicine staff can add brief mental health screening to preseason and injury-rehabilitation pathways, and make a clinician with sport experience accessible. Because anxiety, stress and depression were linked to later injury in several cohorts, staff should consider mood and stress alongside injury monitoring, while recognising that the associations are observational.
paper.athleteDev: Depression was associated with performance failure in cited studies of elite swimmers, and depressive symptoms or perceived stress with later time lost to illness in Australian Olympic athletes. Mental wellbeing therefore belongs in performance planning, with concerns routed to a qualified clinician rather than handled through performance monitoring alone.
paper.rtp: Psychological readiness and preinjury stress were associated with return to sport and rehabilitation outcomes in cited surgical studies, so mental state is worth assessing during rehabilitation. The review does not provide validated psychological criteria for return to sport, so it cannot set a clearance threshold.

records.sourceFile: How to tackle mental fatigue - A systematic review of potential countermeasures and their underlying mechanisms.pdf

paper.citation: Proost M, Habay J, De Wachter J, De Pauw K, Rattray B, Meeusen R, et al. How to Tackle Mental Fatigue: A Systematic Review of Potential Countermeasures and Their Underlying Mechanisms. Sports Med. 2022.
paper.abstract: The authors systematically reviewed acute countermeasures against mental fatigue, classified by timing (before, during or after the fatiguing task) and type (behavioural, physiological or psychological). Of 33 included studies, most countermeasures improved behavioural or subjective markers of mental fatigue, but the neurophysiological evidence was inconclusive.
paper.tldr: Caffeine, odours, music and extrinsic motivation are the most evidenced countermeasures for mental fatigue, based on small trials in healthy adults. The effects on brain and physiological markers are not yet clear, so these results should guide testing rather than set protocols.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review searching PubMed, Web of Science and PsycINFO to 7 March 2022, with backward and forward citation screening. Eligible studies were RCTs or non-randomised controlled trials in healthy adults aged 18 to 50, with mental fatigue induced by a task of at least 30 minutes, placebo or control groups, and at least two of behavioural, subjective and physiological markers. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and RoB 2 for crossover trials.
paper.findings: Of the 33 studies, 8 tested behavioural, 22 physiological, 1 psychological and 2 combined countermeasures. Most reported positive effects on behavioural or subjective markers, for example caffeine at 5 mg/kg improving endurance or time-trial performance in two small studies (n = 8 and n = 12). Neurophysiological markers were measured in 19 studies, with heterogeneous results, so no firm conclusion was reached. Risk of bias was high in 25 studies, some concerns in 3, and low in 5.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneous fatigue-inducing tasks and markers prevented a meta-analysis. Most studies had small samples and high risk of bias. Several outcomes were cognitive tasks rather than sport performance, and three studies did not report participant sex. Some supporting studies were industry-supported, such as the two chicken essence trials.
paper.practicalImplications: Caffeine taken before a mentally demanding task, odours during the task, and music or motivational incentives are the most promising options to test in your own setting. Caffeine carries gastrointestinal and tremor risks at higher doses, and modafinil is banned in competition. Test any countermeasure with your own athletes and tasks before relying on it, since the evidence comes mostly from small laboratory trials in healthy adults.
paper.athleteDev: Caffeine given relative to body mass, odours during a fatiguing task, and music or extrinsic motivation are the most promising options in this review for managing mental fatigue. Use them as hypotheses to test, since the trials used healthy adults and laboratory tasks. Check WADA rules before using any substance.
paper.rtp: The review addresses acute mental fatigue in healthy adults and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Intermediary role of mental toughness beliefs on the relationship between pain self-efficacy and fear avoidance in Elite injured athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Tawil S, Kassis V, Bassil T, Farhat K, Hourani E, Massoud L, et al. Intermediary role of mental toughness beliefs on the relationship between pain self-efficacy and fear avoidance in Elite injured athletes. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025;17:124.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study of 172 injured elite and competitive athletes in Lebanon examined relationships between fear avoidance, pain self-efficacy and mental toughness. Fear avoidance was negatively correlated with both mental toughness and pain self-efficacy, and mental toughness was positively correlated with pain self-efficacy.
paper.tldr: Among 172 injured athletes, lower fear avoidance went with higher mental toughness and higher pain self-efficacy. The design is cross-sectional, so these are associations, not evidence that mental toughness mediates recovery.
paper.methods: An online cross-sectional survey, completed February to June 2024, of injured elite and competitive athletes recruited through a university sports federation. Participants completed the Athletic Fear Avoidance Questionnaire, Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire and Sports Mental Toughness Questionnaire, analysed with t-tests, ANOVA and Pearson or Spearman correlations.
paper.findings: Of 172 athletes, 57.6% had returned to sport less than a month earlier, and fear avoidance was negatively correlated with mental toughness (r = -0.47) and pain self-efficacy (r = -0.44). Mental toughness differed by sport, highest in boxers (43.5) and lowest in futsal players (35.9). Athletes who had returned within a month scored higher on pain self-efficacy (39.9 vs 35.3, p = 0.016) and mental toughness (42.4 vs 40.3, p = 0.037) and lower on fear avoidance (24.3 vs 27.3, p = 0.009) than those who had not returned.
paper.limitations: The authors note a small, non-random sample limited to elite or competitive athletes, with possible recall and social desirability bias. The Abstract says age and training hours 'predicted' higher mental toughness, but only bivariate tests were run, and in Table 4 the youngest group scored highest, contrary to the Discussion's claim that mental toughness rises with age. The Table 4 age and training-hours means (about 37-39) do not fit the overall mean of 41.5, and the training-hours row repeats the same values under fear avoidance, so those rows look erroneous; the Abstract gives the mental toughness and pain self-efficacy correlation as 0.36 and Results as 0.37.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff working with injured athletes may find it useful to ask about fear avoidance, pain self-efficacy and mental toughness together, since they were associated in this sample. The authors conclude that mental toughness and pain self-efficacy training yield benefits, but no training was tested, so any mental-skills programme should be evaluated rather than assumed to help.
paper.athleteDev: Mental toughness differed by sport and was highest in boxing. The reported higher score in athletes training 10 or more hours a week comes from a table row that appears inconsistent, and the study measured no performance outcome, so the Discussion's link to sports performance is not shown.
paper.rtp: Athletes who had returned to training within a month scored lower on fear avoidance and higher on pain self-efficacy and mental toughness than those who had not returned. The cross-sectional design cannot show that these scores predict return to sport, and the paper should not be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Intersection of race and socioeconomic status on concussion recovery among NCAA student-athletes - A CARE Consortium Study.pdf

paper.citation: Boltz AJ, Memmini AK, Brett BL, Snedden TR, Yengo-Kahn AM, Chandran A, et al. Intersection of Race and Socioeconomic Status on Concussion Recovery among NCAA Student-Athletes: A CARE Consortium Study. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2023;55(12):2180-2193.
paper.abstract: This CARE Consortium cohort study described race and household income in 22,819 NCAA varsity athletes and compared time to return to learn, start of the RTP protocol, RTP protocol completion and unrestricted RTP among athletes with a concussion. Race was not associated with return to learn or start of the RTP protocol, but non-Black/non-White athletes were less likely to complete the RTP protocol and Black athletes were more likely to reach unrestricted RTP than White athletes. The authors conclude that clinicians should be aware of how implicit or preconceived biases may influence concussion management.
paper.tldr: In this large NCAA cohort, most athletes were White and from higher-income households, and race had little relationship with time to return to learn. Small race-related differences were seen in RTP protocol completion and time to unrestricted RTP, and the paper does not explain why.
paper.methods: Data came from the CARE Consortium, a 30-site study of NCAA and military academy athletes, with baseline assessment and post-injury follow-up between 2014 and 2020. Race and household income were self-reported, and SRC was diagnosed by local medical teams using a common definition. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox models estimated time to return to learn (n = 1,724), time to start the RTP protocol, RTP protocol duration and time to unrestricted RTP, adjusting for sex, contact level, SRC history, symptom change and time to asymptomatic.
paper.findings: Most athletes were White (75%), and 53% reported household income above $120,000, whereas 41% of Black athletes reported income below $60,000. In adjusted models, race was not associated with return to learn or start of the RTP protocol (overall p = 0.09). Non-Black/non-White athletes had lower hazard of RTP protocol completion (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.97), and Black athletes had higher hazard of unrestricted RTP (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.31) than White athletes, with Kaplan-Meier medians differing by about 1 day. In both return-to-learn models, stratified by symptom change, taking more than 7 days to become asymptomatic was linked to slower return to learn (HR 0.35), and in the higher symptom-change stratum male athletes returned faster than female athletes (HR 1.31, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.53).
paper.limitations: Race was self-reported and grouped into three categories that combine several different groups, ethnicity was not analysed, and household income was self-reported and not modelled in the recovery analyses. Most SRC in the sample occurred in White athletes, the authors state the findings may not be relevant to the general population, and the analyses did not control for individual sport. The Methods text reports a final dataset of 2,464 SRC for the RTP analyses, whereas the abstract and Tables 1C and 2B give N = 2,646 (with 2,334, 2,083 and 2,267 per outcome), so the exact analytic sample is unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians should not assume that race predicts how quickly an athlete will return to learn after a concussion, since no race difference was found in the adjusted return-to-learn models. The small race differences in RTP protocol completion and unrestricted RTP timing support the authors' call to examine how bias may affect concussion care, but they do not show which athletes need different management. Taking more than 7 days to become asymptomatic was consistently linked to slower return to learn, so prolonged symptoms are a reasonable flag for academic support planning.
paper.athleteDev: This paper addresses concussion recovery and social factors rather than performance development, so it has limited direct use for training or performance programming. It may matter for staff who make decisions about academic and sport workload after concussion.
paper.rtp: It can inform the understanding of time to return to learn, RTP protocol start and completion, and time to unrestricted RTP in collegiate athletes after SRC. It cannot be used to set individual return-to-play criteria or timelines, and the paper does not show that race should change how an individual athlete is managed.
